note: Rabbit Hole originals: fictional characters, labelled as such in the app. Their stories are dramatised, the facts in them are from the case files.

cast.name: Dot
cast.bio: Forty years of listening to the sky.
cast.script: I spent forty years listening to the sky on a radio, and I still think about one night. August fifteenth, 1977. The Big Ear telescope in Ohio picked up a signal so strong and so narrow that the astronomer circled it and wrote one word: Wow! Seventy-two seconds. Then nothing. People have pointed telescopes at that patch of sky again and again. It has never come back. I'm not saying it was aliens. I'm saying nobody has explained it.

cast.name: Rosa
cast.bio: Family history, the kind they don't teach.
cast.script: My great-grandmother painted watch dials in New Jersey in the 1920s. The paint glowed because it had radium in it. The girls were told to shape their brushes with their lips, to get a fine point. The company said it was safe. It wasn't. Women's jaws crumbled. Some died young. A group of them sued, and in 1928 they settled. Their fight helped workers win the right to sue over what a job does to their body. When people say nobody covers things up, I think about her.

cast.name: Mika
cast.bio: I hike to the places in the stories.
cast.script: Last winter I hiked to Dyatlov Pass in the northern Urals. In February 1959, nine experienced hikers cut their way out of their own tent and went out into minus thirty, half dressed. For sixty years people blamed aliens, the army, even a yeti. Standing on that slope, you understand the other answer. In 2021, scientists showed how a small slab of snow could break loose above a tent. Small enough to leave few traces. Big enough to make you run. It still gives me chills.

cast.name: Theo
cast.bio: Declassified documents, read so you don't have to.
cast.script: I read declassified documents for fun. Here's the one that changed how I see everything. March 1962. Operation Northwoods. America's Joint Chiefs of Staff signed a memo proposing fake attacks. A staged hijacking. A ship blown up at Guantanamo. A terror campaign in Miami. All to be blamed on Cuba. Kennedy's team said no. We only know because it was declassified in 1997. So when someone tells me they'd never do that, I say: they wrote it down.

cast.name: Dave
cast.bio: Twenty years in salvage. Ask me about the sea floor.
cast.script: I spent twenty years in commercial salvage, so this one gets me. In 1968 a Soviet submarine, K-129, sank in the Pacific. The CIA wanted it. So they built a giant ship and told the world it belonged to Howard Hughes and was mining the ocean floor. In 1974 they lowered a claw about five kilometres down and lifted part of the sub. The cover story worked. And the ship's name still lives on. A Glomar response means: we can neither confirm nor deny.

cast.name: Bea
cast.bio: Local. I know where the lights are.
cast.script: I grew up next to Rendlesham Forest in Suffolk. In December 1980, American airmen from the base said they saw strange lights coming down through the trees. Their deputy commander wrote a memo to the Ministry of Defence, and people started calling it Britain's Roswell. Here's what nobody from outside tells you. Back then, from that forest at night, you could see the Orford Ness lighthouse flashing through the pines. I'm not saying that explains everything. I'm saying start there.

cast.name: Hal
cast.bio: I collect old lightbulbs. Stay with me.
cast.script: I collect old lightbulbs. Sounds dull. Stay with me. In 1924 the biggest bulb makers in the world, including Osram and Philips, formed a cartel called Phoebus. They agreed a bulb should last a thousand hours, down from about two and a half thousand. And they fined each other if bulbs lasted too long. Meanwhile, a bulb in a fire station in Livermore, California, has been glowing since 1901. They don't make them like that anymore. For a while, that was on purpose.

cast.name: Cat
cast.script: I'm an amateur codebreaker, and this is the one we all grew up on. In 1969 the Zodiac killer mailed a three hundred and forty character cipher to the San Francisco Chronicle. For fifty-one years, nobody could read it. Then in December 2020, three amateurs cracked it. A software developer in Virginia, a mathematician in Australia, and a warehouse worker in Belgium. The message taunted the police. The killer has still never been identified. But amateurs did that. Remember it, next time someone tells you that you can't figure things out.

cast.name: Ray
cast.bio: Grew up under the Nevada sky.
cast.script: I grew up in southern Nevada, and every kid I knew had a UFO story. Lights too high, too fast, too quiet. Turns out we were half right. Out at Groom Lake, the CIA was testing the U-2 spy plane, flying higher than any airliner. Its silver wings caught the sunset long after the ground went dark. The CIA later said its spy planes explain a lot of the UFO reports from back then. They only admitted Area 51 existed in 2013. We weren't crazy. We were looking at secrets.

cast.name: Kai
cast.script: I've sailed through the Bermuda Triangle thirty-one times. Here's my report. Weather. The Gulf Stream is fast, storms build quickly, and it's one of the busiest stretches of ocean on Earth. More boats means more accidents. Studies have found no more ships go missing there than anywhere else that busy. The name itself came from a magazine story in 1964. The Triangle isn't swallowing ships. It's selling books.
